Part of what makes the grid work is almost perfectly matching demand with supply. Utilities use modelling data, trends from what the load was on this day over the past X number of years, weather reports and so on to predict what the load will be. Most of that load is met with power generated by coal facilities. These coal facilities have a slow ramp-up/down time, you can't just throw them onto the grid instantly, and you can't just pull 'em off without potentially damaging equipment. Wind and solar, by contrast, aren't hampered by such restrictions, so they're used when it's safe to do so, and kicked off when not needed.

It's really hard to store energy - it's possible with a big battery pack (like the one Tesla sells now) for a home, but not on a national scale, not with the amounts of power a country (or even a continent, since e.g. Europe has interconnected national grids) generates. The only reasonable way of storing such a huge amount of energy is this, but there's a limited amount of locations for these plants, and building one is a massive ecological problem (you pretty much have to blow the top off a mountain).

You also can't really just get rid of excess energy in a reasonable way; you'd have to boil a huge lake or something like that.

So, you can't get rid of excess power, and you can't store it. The only other alternative is that the grid becomes overloaded and starts failing, usually in a very catastrophic way. Imagine the grid as a hose (or a set of hoses) and energy as water; if you try to push too much water into the system, the hoses will start to burst.

Traditionally, power companies would compensate for that by regulating how much power each powerplant provides. Traditional (coal, gas, nuclear) plants don't run at full power all the time, their output fluctuates based on the current demand in the grid. For example, in winter at night, you'll have low demand - everyone's sleeping. On a hot summer day, everyone runs AC and big factories are running, too, so the demand is high.

The problem with solar panels (and wind power) is that you can't regulate them; especially if they're spread out (e.g. everyone has panels on the roof) instead of being a single facility. With home solar becoming more widespread, power companies have many more sources of power they can't control very well, and it makes it exceedingly difficult to keep the grid running. These small renewable sources can provide energy at a time when nobody wants it, which means that the power company has to get rid of it somehow, which is the first way renewable energy is expensive.

Here in Europe, we have an energy market that works very similarly to the stock market - the price for a megawatt of energy fluctuates based on supply and demand and national providers bid for it. However, unlike the stock market, it's not uncommon for a certain provider to actually pay someone to take their energy, because they have way more than they need, and they need to get rid of it. As the grid becomes less predictable (due to more small unregulated sources being included), this becomes more common.

The second way renewables are expensive is the opposite of the above. Above I was talking about how they can provide energy when nobody needs it, and then you have to pay someone to take it from you. The other problem is that they may not provide energy when it's needed. To compensate for that, you can either buy someone else's excess energy on the market - but that's expensive, because in high-demand times nobody will pay you to take theirs away, they'll charge you a lot instead)... or you can run your own coal-fired or gas-fired powerplants and have them serve as a backup for when renewables fail to deliver what you need. This is partially what Germany started doing after closing their nuclear powerplants; they like to pretend they're going green and eco-conscious, but in reality they built several new gas plants at a great expense.
